tier_reason: README Benchmark section shows fast-http 0.086s vs joyent/http-parser (C) 0.108s ('1.25 times faster') for 100,000 parses of one request header. The benchmark code is public (t/benchmark.lisp run-ll-benchmark; C driver listed in the README) and the C side states gcc -O3, but the hardware is only 'Travis CI' with no CPU model, so this first-party result is C, not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: fast-http: SBCL 1.2.6 (no extra Lisp optimize settings stated in README). http-parser (C): bench driver built with 'gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -Wno-error=unused-but-set-variable -O3'; http_parser.o built with http-parser's own 'make http_parser.o' (Makefile flags not shown); gcc version unstated
corrections.workload: Parsing the same 430-byte HTTP GET request header (request line plus 9 headers) 100,000 times: fast-http run-ll-benchmark (parse-request with empty callbacks, timed by SBCL `time`) vs a C loop of http_parser_init + http_parser_execute with null callbacks (timed by clock())
corrections.caveats: Repo has no LICENSE file; MIT is declared in the README License section and in fast-http.asd's :license field. The benchmark ran on Travis CI with no CPU model stated and uses SBCL 1.2.6 (2014-era), so it has not been re-run for the current release. The gcc version is unstated. The two sides use different timers (SBCL `time` real time vs C clock()). Only one ~430-byte request was tested.

notes: Numbers and the 1.25x ratio match the README exactly. The record said the C compiler flags were unstated, but the README shows gcc -O3 for the driver; I corrected that and the request size (430 bytes, not ~500). Metadata checked via gh GraphQL: 362 stars, not archived, not a fork, no detected license, last commit 2026-04-06 (v0.3.0), so active.

tier_reason: First-party blog post (2026-02-21) gives Criterion head-to-head numbers against httparse 1.10: raw tokenization 1.25x/1.15x/1.11x, parse plus extraction 1.38x/1.46x, header lookup 32-37x. There is no public benchmark code and no CPU, OS, compiler or flags, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 1.11-1.25x faster raw tokenization vs httparse 1.10 (page: 1.25x on small 35B, 42 vs 52 ns; 1.15x on medium 368B, 1.71 vs 1.49 GiB/s; 1.11x on large 733B, 1.63 vs 1.47 GiB/s); 1.38x (220 vs 304 ns) and 1.46x (413 vs 604 ns) faster when equal semantic extraction work is included; 32-37x faster header lookup (0.59-0.67 ns O(1) vs 20.5-23.1 ns O(n))
corrections.caveats: No public source repository found. The github.com/SynapServe organization has 0 public repositories (checked via GraphQL and the org page), and no synapserve crate is on crates.io. The site claims an 'open core' with SynapServe Core 'Open Source, Free' under an unnamed open-source license, but the page footer says '© 2026 SynapServe. All rights reserved.' So has_code, usability and license cannot be confirmed. No CPU model, OS, compiler or build flags are stated. The page is internally inconsistent: the comparison table gives medium parse as '200 ns (incl. semantics)', but the equal-work section gives 220 ns. The baseline (httparse) is a widely used incumbent, but it is not one of the three named assignment baselines (llhttp, http-parser, picohttpparser). The site is an investor-pitch page for a commercial product.

notes: All claimed numbers appear on the page. The only correction is that the page gives 1.25x for small requests, so the raw range is 1.11-1.25x, not 1.11-1.15x. SynapServe has no public code (GitHub org empty, crates.io 404). The only GitHub search hit, h-h-v/synapserve, is an unrelated Python ITSM ML project. Kept at C with has_code=false and usability=reference; I did not reject because the baseline is recognizable and the numbers exist.
